title: Consistent Hashing
summary:
Place nodes and keys on the same hash ring (`0 … 2^m − 1`). A key belongs to the **first node token clockwise** from its hash. Adding a node takes over only the arc next to it; every other key stays put.

```
A(10) ---- B(40) ---- C(80) ---- wrap        keys in (10,40] → B
A(10) - D(25) - B(40) ---- C(80) ---- wrap   keys in (10,25] → D, the rest unchanged
```

**Scaling out** differs by what the node holds:
- **Cache:** no migration. Moved keys just miss and refill.
- **Database:** must migrate. New node joins as *joining* → the key range is copied while traffic still goes to the old node → once caught up, switch traffic → the old node deletes its copy.

**Use it** when you want key affinity (the same key almost always lands on the same shard: caches, KV stores) and when the node count changes freely, because rebalancing moves the minimum. **Don't** use it to route to stateful backends that own sessions or in-flight work; route those explicitly. In practice each node gets many virtual tokens so load evens out.

drills.q: With N nodes on a hash ring and one node added, roughly what fraction of keys move?
drills.explain: Only the arc the new node claims moves. With `hash(key) % N`, adding a node remaps almost every key — the problem consistent hashing solves.

drills.q: Ring: A at 10, B at 40, C at 80; a key belongs to the first token clockwise. D joins at 25. Which keys change owner?
options: Keys hashing into (10, 25], moving from B to D
Keys hashing into (10, 25], moving from A to D
Keys hashing into (25, 40], moving from B to D
drills.explain: Before D, (10, 40] belonged to B. D now owns (10, 25]. A and C are untouched. (Some systems use the opposite convention — say which one you use.)

drills.q: Order the steps for adding a node to a consistent-hashed **database**.
items: New node joins the ring marked as joining
Its key range is copied from the old owner while reads and writes still go to the old owner
Once it has caught up, traffic for the range switches to the new node
The old owner deletes its copy of the range
drills.explain: A cache can skip the copy (misses refill it); a database cannot, or reads would return nothing.

drills.q: Where is consistent hashing a good fit?
options: A distributed cache whose node count changes with load
A KV store that wants each key on a stable shard
Routing requests to the server that holds a user's live WebSocket session
Balancing stateless HTTP requests evenly across identical servers
drills.explain: It shines for key affinity with a changing node set. Stateful routing needs an explicit owner lookup (a ring rebalance would silently move sessions), and stateless requests just need round-robin or least-loaded.

drills.q: A cache cluster grows from 9 to 10 nodes with consistent hashing (many virtual nodes each). About what percentage of keys miss because they moved?
drills.explain: About 1/10 of the ring is handed to the new node, so ≈ 10% of keys move. With `% N` it would be ≈ 90%.

drills.q: Why do real systems give each node many virtual tokens instead of one?
drills.answer: With one token per node, arcs are uneven, so load is uneven, and a leaving node dumps its whole arc onto a single neighbour. Many virtual tokens per node make each node's share close to 1/N and spread a departing node's load across many nodes. Weights are easy too: more tokens for bigger machines.
